en: <1>The 7 problems behind this door</1>
<1>I was pushed to pay</1>
The offer rushed you, the odds or the real cost were hidden, or the rule that weighed against you was buried in the terms of use.

It tends to emerge as an operating programme, that is, as an articulation of multiple mechanisms that compress time for reflection, reorganise expectation, increase the cost of exit, hinder reversal and make enjoyment progressively dependent on the very environment that governs it.<1>p. 670</1>
<1>The 5 problems behind this door</1>
<1>I want to leave and take what is mine</1>
Leaving seems free, but it costs the history, the reputation, what you bought and the people you met there. That cost counts too.
Power is not stabilised only by price, but by the cost of exit.<1>p. 217</1>

Leaving means abandoning history, reputation, library, items, progression, emotional investments, networks of sociability and, in certain cases, the very ability to take part in communities that organise themselves within that ecosystem.<1>p. 217</1>
<1>The 2 problems behind this door</1>
<1>The platform decides about me without explaining</1>
Reach dropped, the app's rule changed or the store punished you without saying why. It applies to those who buy, and also to those who sell or work there.
What decides is the real structure of subjection, not the contractual appearance of horizontality.<1>p. 780</1>
<1>The 4 problems behind this door</1>
<1>Prove and complain</1>
Whatever the door, the time comes to prove what happened and to complain where the answer counts.

1. This trust does not arise on its own from good service. Often it is produced, adjusted and maintained by the design of the screen and of customer service.
2. In a service you use every day, small frustrations are absorbed and stop looking like a problem. They start to look like the normal working of the system.

3. Trust does not need to come as a formal guarantee to have an effect. It is enough that it leads you to put up with friction, accept vague justifications, find a loss normal and keep using the service even when it has already got worse.
1. You ask, the assistant answers, and you use the answer to decide something, whether writing a text, solving a work question or understanding a contract.

2. What you use depends on many things on the other side. It depends on the system staying online, the screen staying similar, the conditions of access, the notices that appear, the memory of the conversation when there is one and the service's internal rules.
3. You enter an environment ruled by the company's rules, policies and guidelines, which it can change, limit and reorganise whenever it wants.

1. It looks as if you are seeing the market or the conversation as they are. But everything reached you already chosen, ordered and highlighted by the platform, with criteria you do not control and can almost never check.
